56 machines · three kinds and some impostors

Perpetuum Mobile

56 machines that claim to run for ever. Physicists sort such machines into three kinds, by the rule each one has to break. On these sheets they do run for ever, because that rule is switched off. Open a machine to read its claim, switch the rule back on, and watch it stop.

56, one per machine

Figs. 1–24

The first kind

Machines that give out more work than they take in. The first law of thermodynamics says energy is never created, so each of these hides a mistake in the bookkeeping.

The second kind

Machines that create no energy. They take heat from surroundings at a single temperature and turn it into work, which the second law of thermodynamics forbids.

The third kind

Machines that keep moving because nothing takes their energy away. They make no claim to give out work, and they fail because some loss always remains.

Figs. 49–56

The impostors

Machines that did run, some for a season and some for centuries, on energy that nobody mentioned. Two were frauds. The rest are honest devices that live off small changes in their surroundings.

In 1775 the Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris resolved to stop examining proposals for perpetual motion. With its rule suspended, each figure here is helped along by an unseen hand. With the rule in force it runs down as the real thing would. The numbers in the readouts are illustrative.
